title: The Balloon That Sailed the Stripes

topics.value_lesson: Carrying something forward: each generation of watchers adds a page to the sketchbook, and we get to add ours

spine: A grandmother's old family sketchbook carries us on a cloud-balloon journey down Jupiter's bands, around the Great Red Spot, and out to the big moons, so we can add our own page before sailing home.

child_name.role: What Grandma Sef and Nix call the child listening, inside the memory

spot_drawing.role: What the child draws on their sketchbook page at the end
spot_drawing.default: the Great Red Spot with a tiny smiling balloon beside it

segments.text:
This book is older than me, and older than my grandma, and maybe older than the hills. Feel the cover. Soft as a dog's ear, isn't it? Every page is a drawing of the same place, added by somebody in our family. And this page at the back is blank. It's waiting.

Let me tell you about the night it nearly got its drawing.

I was about your age, and Grandma Sef finally said I was old enough to sail the whole route with her. Her balloon was called the Stripe, and it floated at the thin, fuzzy edge of space, right above Jupiter.

Jupiter is a gas giant, {child_name}. That means it's all clouds, top to bottom. No ground anywhere. Nothing to stand on, ever. Just cloud bands, stripes of cream and rust and gold, sliding past each other slow as honey.

Nix was there too, counting moons in his tally notebook. "Seventy-nine! Eighty!" he kept saying. And Stir the robot was cooking something that smelled like tomato soup.

Grandma Sef patted the sketchbook. "One full route," she said, "and the page is yours."

"Up we go!" Grandma Sef said, and the Stripe lifted to the very top of the highest cloud band. We sailed the stripes like a train on tracks. "Cream station!" Grandma Sef called. "Tan station! Rust station!" Nix pressed his nose to the glass. "What comes after rust? I want to guess right." "Guess," said Grandma Sef. Nix squeezed his eyes shut. "Blue?" "Pale blue-grey," Grandma Sef announced, "next station!" Nix whooped. "I nearly said grey!" Grandma Sef pointed at the stripes sliding past each other. "The light ones blow one way, the dark ones blow back, side by side, like two rivers running opposite ways." Stir dinged a little bell. "Soup! Stripe-swirled soup!" It was swirled cream and rust, just like the clouds. "Jupiter's whole day is only ten hours," said Grandma Sef. "So it's breakfast again already." Nix counted on his fingers. "Again?" We drank our soup while the stripes hurried past, faster and faster. "Wait," said Nix, leaning forward. "What's after rust? I forgot already!"

"Down we go," Grandma Sef said softly, and the Stripe sank toward the deep orange mist. We hovered above it. The fog turned slowly, thick as tomato soup, as porridge, as the jam at the bottom of the jar. Grandma Sef pressed her hand flat to the bubble window. "Feel, {child_name}. No floor out there. Just fog turning to soup, all the way down." Nix leaned so far out his nose nearly touched the glass. "But if there's no ground anywhere, what's holding us up?" Stir handed us cocoa, warm in our hands. "The balloon floats on Jupiter's breath," Stir said, "the way a leaf floats on a pond." Nix looked at his cocoa, then at the mist. "So we're a leaf?" "A very cozy leaf," said Grandma Sef. I watched the fog curl far below, slow and orange, and wondered what it would feel like to dip a finger in. "Would it feel like bathwater?" I asked. "Warm," said Grandma Sef, "and thick, and it would hold you like soup holds a spoon."

Back on the route, something is growing over the curve of the world. A dot. A coin. A dinner plate. Until it fills the whole round window, edge to edge.

"There she is," says Grandma Sef. "The Great Red Spot."

It isn't red, really. It's orange, deep and warm, turning slow as syrup. A swirl bigger than the whole Earth, just turning and turning in the clouds.

Grandma Sef opens the sketchbook, soft as a dog's ear, to a page near the front. "My great-grandmother drew this. The very same swirl. It's been turning for hundreds of years, {child_name}. Since long before anyone we know was born."

"Hundreds?" says Nix, looking up from his tally notebook. "That's more than all my moons."

We drift along the rim, where the orange clouds curl like the top of tomato soup. Stir says the soup is ready, and nobody answers, because nobody wants to look away.

"Watch," Grandma Sef whispers. "It moves. But only if you're patient."

So we watch. And the Spot turns, slow and sure, like it has all the time in the world.

Then Nix sits up straight. "Dots! Bright dots, ahead!" His pencil is already moving. "Moons, {child_name}. Big ones. Waiting to be counted."

The Stripe bumps, soft as a kiss, against the moon-hopper station. "Out we hop," says Grandma Sef.

We step onto the big moon, and the ground is real and still and dusty under our boots. And there, filling half the black sky, hangs Jupiter. Striped. Enormous. Close enough to touch, almost.

"Moons!" shouts Nix, notebook already open. "Count with me, {child_name}. Io, with its orange volcano fountains, fizzing like a pot that boils over. Europa, white and cracked as old ice on a pond. Ganymede. Callisto. Four!" He presses a sticker into my hand. "For your tally."

"Europa looks like a skating pond," I say.

"Under the ice?" Nix grins. "A whole secret ocean. Hiding."

The radio operator waves us past her window. "Before you go — look." She points. On her fingertip, a tiny blue dot. "Earth. That's home, that is."

Home. That little.

Back aboard, Grandma Sef opens the sketchbook, soft as a dog's ear, to the blank page at the back. "Yours," she says.

So I draw. {spot_drawing}. Nix sticks my sticker in the corner. Stir brings soup.

And that, my love, is the end of the remembering. Because this book on your lap — this very one, soft as a dog's ear — is that book. And this page, still warm from my hand, is the page I drew that night, when I was about your age.

"Stay aboard it is," says Grandma Sef, and the Stripe turns its nose toward the dark.

The map room is at the back, where the windows go black as bedtime. Nix flips a switch. And the whole room blooms — seventy-nine tiny lights, one for every moon, glowing like fireflies in a jar.

"Seventy-nine," Nix breathes. "All of them. But which line is the way home?"

Then a golden dotted line draws itself through the lights, curving between the moons, slow and sure. "That one," says Grandma Sef. "It always knows."

"Breakfast!" calls Stir. "Timed to the minute. Jupiter spins so fast, a whole day there is ten hours. Eat slow, and the sunrise comes back around before you've finished."

So we eat tomato soup, and watch the light creep over the cloud bands, gold on cream on rust. A whole sunrise, before the bowls are empty. Nix licks his spoon. "Best timed breakfast ever," he says.

We lay our souvenirs in a row on the table. A jar of cloud-banded light. My drawing of the Spot. Nix's moon stickers. The whole trip, in a row.

Then Grandma Sef opens the sketchbook, soft as a dog's ear, to the blank page at the back. "Yours," she says.

So I draw. {spot_drawing}.

And that, my love, is the end of the remembering. Because this book on your lap is that book. And the page you're looking at right now — that's the page I drew, when I was about your age.

gathered_but_unused: Jupiter is a gas giant, which means it has no solid ground — it is clouds and gas all the way down, getting thicker and thicker like fog turning into soup.
Jupiter is so big that more than a thousand Earths could fit inside it.
The stripes on Jupiter are called cloud bands, and the light ones and dark ones are winds blowing in opposite directions, side by side.
The Great Red Spot is a single swirling storm bigger than the whole Earth, and it has been turning for hundreds of years.
The Great Red Spot has been spinning since before your great-great-great-grandparents were born — astronomers have watched it through telescopes for hundreds of years.
Jupiter spins faster than any other planet — one whole day on Jupiter is only about ten hours long.
Jupiter has at least 79 moons, and four of them are so big you could see them from your backyard with just binoculars.
One of Jupiter's big moons, Io, is covered in volcanoes, and another, Europa, hides an ocean of liquid water under its smooth icy shell.
